title: The Sham Of High Expectations
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In one of his more pointed pieces, Linsin argues that most schools' talk of 'high expectations' is a sham, as behavior standards continue eroding under an educational culture uncomfortable with consequences. He describes a cycle where disruptive students face minimal real accountability—brief office visits, counseling, a talking-to—before returning to class where teachers are pressured to praise and reward minimal improvement rather than enforce genuine standards. He argues this approach, dressed up as research-based, actually worsens behavior over time while punishing well-behaved students who quietly absorb the resulting disorder. His counter-argument is that firm, clearly defined, consistently enforced boundaries are what make students feel safe and cared for, and that true caring means holding students accountable rather than repeatedly excusing them.
points: Argues that institutional talk of 'high expectations' is largely a sham as real behavior standards continue to erode.
Describes minimal-accountability discipline cycles—brief office visits and counseling—that return disruptive students to class unchanged.
Contends reward-based, 'research-based' classroom management systems worsen behavior over time despite occasional short-term compliance.
Argues firm, consistently enforced boundaries make students feel safe and cared for, not oppressed.
Redefines true caring as making hard, accountability-driven decisions rather than repeatedly excusing misbehavior.
quotes: The truth is, for the most part, it’s a sham. Expectations for student behavior in this day and age are knee-high to a five year old.

You’re asked to rely on one of the several trendy “research-based” classroom management systems your school has adopted that reject true accountability, replacing it with extrinsic rewards and appeasement.

Except for the occasional temporary improvement (e.g. students getting quiet or sitting up straight) that can happen in exchange for a reward or false praise—hence the “research”—behavior worsens over time.

All students need firmly established, nonnegotiable boundaries. If they don’t have them, in the form of clearly defined rules and their consequences, then they’ll push and probe and test until they find them.
Caring isn’t giving chance after chance. It isn’t looking the other way or excusing behavior you know is wrong. It isn’t pretending everything is okay while Rome burns.
You do right by students, and their families who have so much hope for them, by establishing boundaries that safeguard excellent teaching and inspired learning.
